pages.text: Madam Sowah held up a photo of giant grey stones standing in a ring on a grassy plain in England. “This is Stonehenge. It was started about five thousand years ago, long before there were cars, cranes or even iron tools. Today’s mystery: how and why?”

“This is Stonehenge.
It was started about five thousand years ago, long before there were cars, cranes or even iron tools.
Today’s mystery: how and why?”
pages.alt: A teacher shows a photograph of Stonehenge on the board.

pages.text: Antwi measured on his ruler. “If the biggest stones weigh many tonnes, how did people move them?” “Good question,” said Madam Sowah. “Some of the stones are called sarsens. Scientists found their likely source: a place about 25 kilometres away.” “Walking distance,” said Nyarko, “but with a rock?”

Scientists found their likely source: a place about 25 kilometres away.” “Walking distance,” said Nyarko, “but with a rock?”
pages.alt: Children measure a stone photo while a map shows a short route.

pages.text: “Nobody wrote down how it was done,” said Madam Sowah. “So scientists suggest ideas, such as pulling the stones on wooden sledges over logs with ropes and teams of people. We do not have a complete, proven answer. It would have taken hundreds of people working together.”

“So scientists suggest ideas, such as pulling the stones on wooden sledges over logs with ropes and teams of people.
We do not have a complete, proven answer.
It would have taken hundreds of people working together.”
pages.alt: People pull a huge stone on a wooden sledge over logs.

pages.text: “Now the surprise,” said Madam Sowah. “Smaller stones, called bluestones, came from hills in Wales, a long way off. And one big stone in the middle, the Altar Stone, was long thought to be from Wales too.” She paused. “In 2024, scientists said it likely came from northeast Scotland, at least 700 kilometres away. It weighs about six tonnes.”

pages.alt: A map of Britain with arrows from Wales and Scotland to Stonehenge.

pages.text: “700 kilometres!” cried Nyarko. “More than the distance from Accra to Tamale!” Antwi checked. Accra to Tamale is a little over 600 kilometres by road. “It is,” he said, “a little more than that.” “That is the longest known journey for a stone in a monument of that age,” said Madam Sowah. “How? By land? By sea? We do not know yet.”

pages.alt: Two boys compare a long road with a map of a stone’s journey.

pages.text: “And why?” asked Antwi. “A calendar? A place for ceremonies? A meeting place? A burial place? Scientists have good ideas, and many are debated,” said Madam Sowah. “For example, some suggest it was built to bring people from different places together, because stones came from across Britain. Nobody can prove the full purpose.”

pages.text: Antwi thought about it. “If hundreds of people pulled one stone, they must have worked as a team,” he said. Madam nodded. “That is what we can say with confidence,” she said. “People worked together on something that mattered to them. Think of Ghanaian villages building a school or a market together.”

pages.text: Madam Sowah asked them to write one thing Stonehenge has taught them. Nyarko wrote: Mysteries can have a few answers and many questions. Antwi wrote: People long ago were clever and worked together. “Exactly,” said Madam Sowah. “And scientists keep learning. Who knows what we will find next?” The end.

activities.question: Where does the Altar Stone likely come from, according to the 2024 study?

activities.prompt: There were no cranes or modern tools. How do you think the builders moved heavy stones?
options: With ropes, wooden sledges and many people working together

activities.question: What can we say with confidence about the builders?
options: They worked together as a team

items: People began building Stonehenge about 5,000 years ago.
Stones were moved from far away.
In 2024, scientists traced the Altar Stone to Scotland.
The reason for Stonehenge is still debated.

activities.prompt: Hundreds of people worked together on Stonehenge. When have you worked with others on something big?
